description: The PTR record for an IPv4 or IPv6 address, and the forward lookup that decides whether it counts. Reverse DNS is delegated to whoever holds the address block, so a PTR alone proves nothing — the operator of an IP can point it at any hostname, including one they do not own. Only the round trip is evidence: PTR names a host, that host resolves back to the same address. That pair is forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS), it is what Google and Yahoo mean when they list forward and reverse DNS among their bulk sender requirements, and it is what `fcrdns` reports. Over IPv6 it is stricter still: Gmail rejects IPv6 mail from an address without it, where the same mail over IPv4 would be accepted. Reports a missing PTR separately from a PTR that fails to confirm, because the fixes differ and only the address block's operator — usually the hosting provider, not the sender — can set either.

ip.description: An IPv4 or IPv6 address, e.g. "8.8.8.8" or "2001:4860:4860::8888". Not a hostname.
